set.explanation: Hypotension, tachycardia, a raised JVP, muffled heart sounds and pulsus paradoxus with a large effusion and right atrial systolic collapse on echo is cardiac tamponade, most likely malignant in a woman with breast cancer. The treatment is urgent echo-guided pericardiocentesis, with fluid sent for cytology, culture and biochemistry. Furosemide (and any venodilator) lowers preload and can precipitate collapse, NSAID/colchicine treats inflammation but not the haemodynamic compromise, and CT only delays drainage; IV fluid can be a temporising bridge but is never a substitute for drainage.

set.stem: A 27-year-old man has had sharp, stabbing chest pain radiating to the shoulder and left jaw for 3 days with a low-grade fever. A to-and-fro scratching sound is heard over the precordium and the ECG shows ST elevation in I, II, aVF and V2–V5. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: Sharp pleuritic/positional pain after a febrile illness, a to-and-fro (friction) rub and concave ST elevation across several coronary territories (inferior and anterior leads together) is acute pericarditis, usually viral or idiopathic. An MI produces ST elevation confined to one territory with reciprocal depression, and myocarditis is suggested by heart failure, arrhythmia or a markedly raised troponin rather than a rub. Echo is needed to look for an effusion, and first-line treatment is aspirin or an NSAID plus colchicine.

Days after acute pericarditis, a new raised JVP, pulsus paradoxus and hypotension (Beck's triad features) mean an effusion has accumulated fast enough to cause tamponade. Heart failure or a cardiomyopathy would give pulmonary congestion and a displaced apex rather than pulsus paradoxus with a sudden drop in BP. Echo confirms it and pericardiocentesis is urgent.

set.stem: A patient with acute pericarditis develops hypotension, a raised JVP and pulsus paradoxus. Which investigation best confirms this complication?
set.explanation: Echocardiography is the key test for suspected tamponade: it shows the effusion, right atrial and right ventricular diastolic collapse, a plethoric IVC and exaggerated respiratory variation in mitral/tricuspid inflow, and it guides pericardiocentesis. The ECG (low voltage, electrical alternans) and chest X-ray (globular heart) are supportive but insensitive and non-specific, and cardiac enzymes and exercise testing have no diagnostic role; tamponade itself remains a clinical-haemodynamic diagnosis confirmed by echo.

Tamponade with hypotension is treated by urgent drainage, usually echo-guided pericardiocentesis (surgical drainage for purulent, clotted or post-cardiac-surgery collections). Diuretics, nitrates and ACE inhibitors reduce preload or afterload and worsen the already limited ventricular filling, and digoxin has no role. Cautious IV fluid may support BP while drainage is arranged.

The prognosis of acute rheumatic fever depends mainly on the severity of carditis and on recurrences, and both are greatest when the first attack occurs in young children (carditis complicates the large majority of attacks in early childhood, and the risk of recurrence falls with increasing age). Attacks beginning in adolescence or adulthood more often present as arthritis without carditis. Absence of valve involvement and normal inflammatory markers are good signs; secondary penicillin prophylaxis is what prevents recurrence and progression to chronic rheumatic heart disease.

why: Source key (old age) is wrong: younger age at first attack carries more carditis and more recurrences, i.e. a worse prognosis

set.explanation: In the modified Duke criteria a major microbiological criterion is persistently positive blood cultures – for example all three or most of four or more separate sets with the first and last at least 1 hour apart (or two sets over 12 hours apart), or typical organisms in two separate sets. A predisposing valve lesion, IV drug use and embolic (vascular) phenomena are all minor criteria. The other major criterion is imaging evidence of endocardial involvement (vegetation, abscess, new dehiscence or new valvular regurgitation).

In tamponade the pericardial pressure raises all diastolic cardiac pressures, so the JVP is markedly raised (with a prominent x and blunted y descent) – a collapsed JVP points instead to hypovolaemia. Hypotension, pulsus paradoxus, muffled heart sounds and low-voltage QRS complexes (sometimes with electrical alternans) are all typical. Beck's triad is hypotension, a raised JVP and quiet heart sounds.

Endocarditis within weeks of valve surgery (early prosthetic valve endocarditis) is usually acquired peri-operatively, and coagulase-negative staphylococci (e.g. Staphylococcus epidermidis) and S. aureus dominate; they form biofilm on prosthetic material. Oral viridans streptococci (S. sanguinis, S. milleri group), S. bovis/gallolyticus and enterococci cause community-acquired native or late prosthetic infection. Treatment is prolonged vancomycin- or flucloxacillin-based therapy with rifampicin and gentamicin, and early surgery is often needed.

set.stem: A middle-aged woman has fatigue, abdominal distension and leg swelling. Her pulse is 112/min, regular and of small volume, there is an early diastolic sound (pericardial knock), and the chest X-ray shows calcification around the heart shadow. Chronic constrictive pericarditis is suspected. Which finding is AGAINST this diagnosis?
set.explanation: Constriction impairs filling of both ventricles and presents mainly with systemic venous congestion – a raised JVP with Kussmaul's sign, marked (often early, disproportionate) ascites, hepatomegaly and leg oedema – while the lungs are usually clear, so prominent orthopnoea/breathlessness suggests left heart failure or another diagnosis. Pericardial calcification and a knock support constriction. Confirmation is by echo, CT/MRI of pericardial thickening and, if needed, simultaneous right- and left-heart catheterisation; definitive treatment is pericardiectomy.

Myocarditis typically presents with chest pain, acute heart failure, arrhythmias or, in fulminant cases, cardiogenic shock, with a raised troponin and often ECG changes. A pericardial rub is a sign of pericardial inflammation and is heard only when there is associated pericarditis (myopericarditis), so it is not a feature of myocarditis itself. Cardiac MRI (oedema and non-ischaemic late gadolinium enhancement) is the key non-invasive test.

Acute rheumatic fever follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis and peaks in children aged 5–15 years, the age group with the most streptococcal throat infections. It is rare under 3 years and uncommon in adults, and does not occur in neonates. It remains common in low- and middle-income countries, where it is the main cause of acquired heart disease in the young.

Acute pericarditis evolves through diffuse concave (saddle-shaped) ST elevation with PR depression, then ST normalisation, then T-wave inversion, then resolution. Hyperacute (tall, broad) T waves are the earliest sign of acute transmural ischaemia in STEMI and are not a feature of pericarditis. Territorial ST elevation with reciprocal depression and Q waves also point to infarction rather than pericarditis.

set.stem: A 22-year-old man has fever, night sweats and weight loss. There are linear (splinter) haemorrhages under the nails and a new pansystolic murmur radiating to the left axilla. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
set.explanation: Constitutional symptoms with a new regurgitant murmur and vascular phenomena (splinter haemorrhages) is infective endocarditis until proven otherwise; the murmur here reflects mitral regurgitation caused by valve destruction. Rheumatic heart disease, a VSD or tricuspid regurgitation would not explain fever, weight loss and embolic signs. At least three sets of blood cultures before antibiotics and echocardiography are the next steps.

set.stem: A 22-year-old man has fever, night sweats and weight loss. There are linear (splinter) haemorrhages under the nails and a new pansystolic murmur radiating to the left axilla. Which investigation should be performed first, before antibiotics are started?
set.explanation: Blood cultures – at least three sets from separate venepunctures before antibiotics – are the most important first investigation in suspected endocarditis because they identify the organism, guide therapy and form a major Duke criterion. Echocardiography (transthoracic, then transoesophageal if needed) is the other major criterion and follows promptly, but a delay in taking cultures or giving antibiotics first can leave the infection culture-negative. FBC, urinalysis (microscopic haematuria) and chest X-ray are supportive only.

set.explanation: Systemic embolisation of vegetation fragments is a major complication of left-sided endocarditis, and the brain is the commonest site, so new focal weakness is most likely an embolic stroke. A ruptured mycotic aneurysm or subarachnoid haemorrhage is much less common and usually presents with sudden headache and reduced consciousness, and an extradural haematoma follows trauma. Urgent brain imaging (CT/MRI) is needed, and embolic events with large vegetations are an indication to consider early surgery.

The main indications for surgery in endocarditis are heart failure due to valve dysfunction, uncontrolled infection (perivalvular abscess, fistula, enlarging vegetation or persistently positive cultures/fever beyond about 7–10 days of appropriate antibiotics, fungal or resistant organisms) and prevention of embolism with large vegetations. Young age in itself is not an indication. Decisions are made by a multidisciplinary endocarditis team.

set.stem: A middle-aged woman presents with fatigue, abdominal distension and light-headedness. Constrictive pericarditis is suspected. Which of the following findings would be LEAST typical of this diagnosis?
set.explanation: Constrictive pericarditis classically gives a raised JVP with a rapid y descent, Kussmaul's sign (JVP rises on inspiration because the rigid pericardium cannot accommodate increased venous return), an early diastolic pericardial knock and prominent ascites. Pulsus paradoxus is the hallmark of cardiac tamponade and is uncommon in pure constriction, where the rigid shell insulates the heart from intrathoracic pressure changes. The key differential is restrictive cardiomyopathy, separated by pericardial thickening on CT/MRI and haemodynamic studies.

set.stem: A 55-year-old man has progressive shortness of breath and ankle oedema. He is originally from Africa and probably had tuberculosis many years ago. His BP is 105/55 mmHg, the JVP is raised 5 cm with a rapid y descent, and there is marked ankle oedema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: Right-sided congestion with a raised JVP showing a steep (rapid) y descent after previous tuberculosis is typical of constrictive pericarditis: the ventricles fill rapidly in early diastole until they hit the rigid pericardium. Tamponade instead abolishes the y descent and causes pulsus paradoxus, and aortic regurgitation gives a wide pulse pressure and an early diastolic murmur. Restrictive cardiomyopathy produces similar haemodynamics, but the TB history favours constriction; CT/MRI showing pericardial thickening or calcification confirms it.

set.stem: Dressler syndrome results from which of the following?
set.explanation: Dressler (post-myocardial infarction) syndrome is an autoimmune pericarditis, often with pleural and pericardial effusions, fever and a raised ESR/CRP, developing weeks after MI as antimyocardial antibodies form against antigens released from damaged myocardium. It is not infective, so antibiotics and antivirals have no role. Treatment is aspirin (or another NSAID once the infarct has healed) with colchicine, glucocorticoids being reserved for refractory cases.

Chest pain after a viral-type illness with distant heart sounds and a newly enlarged cardiac silhouette indicates acute (viral) pericarditis with a pericardial effusion; the heart shadow becomes globular once more than about 200–250 mL has accumulated. LV hypertrophy barely changes the silhouette, dilated cardiomyopathy would give heart failure signs and a gallop, and pulmonary oedema causes perihilar shadowing rather than a larger heart shadow. Echocardiography confirms the effusion and assesses for tamponade.

set.stem: A 21-year-old man has a recent influenza-like illness with fever, myalgia and headache. He then develops pleuritic-type chest discomfort and breathlessness. His pulse is 105/min and regular and BP is 105/60 mmHg; the JVP is not raised. The first and second heart sounds are normal, and a loud, harsh to-and-fro sound is heard in both systole and diastole. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: A scratchy to-and-fro sound in both systole and diastole after a viral illness with pleuritic pain is a pericardial friction rub from acute viral pericarditis; the normal JVP indicates no tamponade. A patent ductus gives a continuous machinery murmur from birth, endocarditis gives a regurgitant murmur with embolic and constitutional features, and pulmonary embolism gives pleuritic pain and hypoxia but no rub over the heart. Treatment is aspirin or an NSAID with colchicine.

First-line treatment of acute pericarditis is high-dose oral aspirin (e.g. 750–1000 mg every 8 hours) or an NSAID such as ibuprofen, tapered over 1–2 weeks, plus colchicine for 3 months to halve the recurrence rate (ESC). Glucocorticoids are second line because they increase recurrence, amiodarone has no role, and opioids only mask symptoms. Rectal diclofenac is an unusual route and not the standard initial therapy.

Tuberculous pericarditis is the commonest cause of constrictive pericarditis worldwide, particularly in TB-endemic regions; other causes are previous cardiac surgery, mediastinal radiotherapy, viral/idiopathic pericarditis and connective tissue disease. Acute MI causes pericarditis that very rarely constricts, and dilated cardiomyopathy, alcohol and osteoarthritis do not cause constriction. Adjunctive glucocorticoids with antituberculous therapy may reduce the risk of constriction in TB pericarditis.
